Brzeg Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Brzeg, Poland

Not demolished. Jews are first recorded in Brzeg at the turn of the 13th-14th century, though they were expelled twice - in 1453 and 1582 - before returning in 1650; an autonomous kehilla formed in 1660. Population reached 140 (3%) by 1782, falling to just 0.9% by 1910. A 1933 boycott and the 1938 Kristallnacht synagogue burning preceded wartime deportations to General Government ghettos. This cemetery's dedication was signed in 1798 though the land transaction only finalized in 1863; the first burial occurred in 1801, the last in 1937. Nazi Germany's Jewish Association was forced to sell the cemetery back to the city during WWII. About 150 matzevot survive, mostly sandstone from the second half of the 19th century, the oldest dated 1806 (memorializing Zanwil, son of Meir from Grodków); inscriptions appear in both Hebrew and German. The site entered Poland's Register of Historical Landmarks (no. 235/89) on December 28, 1989.
